summary:
Dmello opens with a provocation: almost everything breaking in production ML security is the same boring infrastructure mistake we supposedly fixed years ago, not exotic AI attacks. She anchors this with a 2023 incident where thousands of Ray clusters were exposed on the public internet because authentication shipped off by default—over a billion dollars at risk, no zero-day required. She traces how ML broke three classical security assumptions: deterministic behavior (now probabilistic), single-tenant serving (now shared multi-tenant GPU), and fixed parameters (now copyable weights leaking through APIs). The LLM stack widens this further: prompts become control flow, answers come from retrieval corpora, and agents take actions.

She distills the field into three core ideas. First, misconfiguration—not missing features—is the number-one failure mode. A 50-system audit found 78% had at least one critical mistake, always the same three: overprivileged accounts, flat networks with no separation, and secrets/weights in publicly reachable storage. She attributes this to security tools built by security experts but handed to ML teams whose priority is model accuracy. Second, defenses that researchers love often do not survive production because every control costs latency and throughput. She tiers controls by overhead: basics like logins and input checking cost under 8% and should always be on; heavier isolation costs 10-20% and can be selective; real-time malicious-input detection costs 15-30% and is often a non-starter. Third, secure ML like infrastructure, not like a model.

She details concrete fixes for the three recurring misconfigurations: least-privilege accounts with short-lived credentials that expire quickly, network segmentation requiring verified identity between services rather than mere network access, and secret managers with encryption and automated scanning before anything ships. She calls this basic hygiene that prevents the breaches that make the news. She then names four emerging threats she is watching: prompt injection (the model cannot distinguish instructions from input), RAG poisoning (a corrupted document store poisons everything downstream), GPU side channels (timing information leaking between co-located customers), and supply-chain risk from downloading unvetted models and add-ons. She cautions that all of this moves fast and defenses are immature. She closes with three takeaways: secure ML as infrastructure, make existing defenses deployable rather than inventing new ones, and fix misconfigurations deliberately while climbing the maturity model. She ties the title back: the LLM stack is a 2008 database with better marketing—lock down access, segment the network, protect data at rest.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Provocation and Ray Cluster Story
sections.summary: Dmello introduces her thesis: production ML security failures are boring infrastructure mistakes, not exotic AI attacks. She opens with the 2023 Ray cluster exposure where authentication was off by default, leaving dashboards and job APIs open, putting over a billion dollars of data at risk.

sections.title: Broken Security Assumptions in ML
sections.summary: Classical 2008 applications were deterministic, single-tenant, and had fixed parameters. ML broke all three assumptions: behavior is probabilistic, weights are copyable, and workloads share multi-tenant GPUs. The LLM stack widens the attack surface further. Security assumptions were never updated.

sections.title: Three Core Ideas and Defense-in-Depth Map
sections.summary: She distills the field into three ideas: misconfiguration is the top failure mode, defenses don't survive production, and ML must be secured like infrastructure. She presents a four-pillar defense-in-depth map (infrastructure, access control, runtime, compliance/culture) and a six-category threat taxonomy.

sections.title: Core Idea One: Misconfiguration Study
sections.summary: An audit of 50 production ML systems found 78% had at least one critical misconfiguration. The same three problems recurred: access controls left wide open, no network separation, and passwords/trained models in publicly reachable storage. She attributes this to security tools built by security experts but operated by ML teams focused on model accuracy.

sections.title: Core Idea Two: Defenses Don't Survive Production
sections.summary: Every control costs latency and throughput. She tiers controls: basics under 8% (always on), heavier isolation 10-20% (selective), and real-time malicious input detection 15-30% (often a non-starter). The key question is how to build controls without slowing everything down, not whether to run them.

sections.title: Ecosystem Gaps and Maturity Model
sections.summary: Three ecosystem gaps: ML security tooling is years behind, expertise silos prevent shared understanding, and research focuses on rare attacks while production fights mundane breaches. She introduces a maturity model with four levels tied to overhead budgets and NIST AI RMF, noting most teams overestimate their maturity. She begins discussing the three specific misconfigurations behind most risk, starting with default admin rights.

sections.title: Three Misconfigurations and Their Fixes
sections.summary: She details fixes for each recurring misconfiguration. For overprivileged accounts: enforce least privilege, ensure each account does only what it needs, and make credentials expire quickly. For flat networks: wall parts from each other and require verified identity between services, not just network access. For exposed secrets and models: use a proper secret manager, encryption, and automatic scanning before shipping. She calls this basic hygiene that prevents the breaches that make the news.

sections.title: Emerging Threats and Final Takeaways
sections.summary: She names four emerging threats she is watching: prompt injection (the model cannot distinguish instructions from input), RAG poisoning (a corrupted document store poisons everything downstream), GPU side channels (timing information leaking between co-located customers), and supply-chain risk from unvetted model downloads. She cautions that defenses are immature and the field moves weekly. She closes with three takeaways: secure ML as infrastructure not a model, make existing defenses deployable rather than inventing new ones, and fix misconfigurations deliberately while climbing the maturity model. She ties the title back: the LLM stack is a 2008 database with better marketing—lock down access, segment the network, protect data at rest.
